today: RFC 9940 is an Informational RFC that establishes standard terminology for network fault and problem management. It has not been obsoleted and is used as a reference in IETF work on YANG data models and management protocols.

sections.title: Why Terminology Matters
sections.content:
Successful operation of large networks requires effective management: detecting problems, gathering information about them, and deciding how to fix them. Network fault and problem management is essential to this process. However, when the IETF works on fault management—in YANG data models, management protocols, and monitoring systems—people use similar words like fault and problem in different ways.

This document defines eight fundamental terms (Event, State, Fault, Problem, Symptom, Cause, Alert, and Alarm) and the relationships between them. These definitions bring clarity to discussions and help ensure that different standards work together consistently. The document is specifically about network fault and problem management at the network layer, though the concepts may also apply at other technology levels.
sections.eli5: When network engineers talk about problems, they need to use the same words to mean the same things. This document is a reference guide.

sections.title: Building Blocks of Fault Management
sections.content:
Fault management starts with resources (elements of a network system, such as links or routers). Each resource has characteristics (observable or measurable aspects, like link status or CPU utilization). Characteristics have values (the actual measurement, such as "up" or "50% utilization").

When a characteristic's value changes, that is a change. When a change is noticed at a distinct moment in time, it is an event. When an event is interpreted according to policy or context, it may be deemed relevant. A relevant event or relevant change is an occurrence.

A condition is an interpretation of one or more characteristic values (for example, "low available memory" or "link degraded"). A state is a particular condition that a resource is in at a specific time. The distinction between a change (which may happen over time) and an event (which happens at a moment in time) is crucial to understanding fault management workflows.
sections.eli5: Networks have parts (resources) with measurable properties (characteristics). Values change. When you notice the change at a specific moment, that is an event. When you interpret it as important, that matters.

sections.title: The Difference Between Fault and Problem
sections.content:
A fault is an undesired occurrence—an event or change that is not wanted. It happens at a moment in time and can potentially be associated with a cause. A link going down is a fault.

A problem is an undesirable state that may require remedial action. Unlike a fault, a problem is ongoing. It may not be directly associated with a cause, and fixing the problem may not fix the thing that has the problem. For example, a link going down is a fault, but the loss of connectivity it causes is a problem. In systems with redundancy, a single link down might be a fault but not a problem (because other links carry traffic). However, a backup power supply failing, leaving the primary unprotected, is both a fault and a problem.

A problem can also be historical: a fault occurred in the recent past and was never explained, and that unexplained fault itself becomes a problem. Problems may be intermittent, recurring, or transient, and they must be actively tracked and resolved.
sections.eli5: A fault is a bad thing that just happened. A problem is a bad situation that is ongoing and needs to be fixed.

sections.title: From Data to Understanding
sections.content:
Network management follows a cascaded sequence. Network telemetry is the collection of operational network data. Network monitoring creates a continuous record of network functions, tracking aspects like traffic patterns, device health, and performance. Network analytics derives insights from that data (such as recognizing that packet loss is high). Network observability enables assessment of network behavior through analysis—identifying deviations between observed state and expected state.

Within this sequence, a symptom is an observable value, change, state, event, or condition that indicates a problem or potential problem. It is evidence of something wrong. A cause is the event or events that gave rise to a fault or problem. Understanding symptoms and causes is how operators identify and fix underlying issues.
sections.eli5: You collect data, watch for patterns, analyze what you see, and understand what is really happening. Symptoms are clues, and causes are the root reasons.

sections.title: Alerts and Alarms
sections.content:
When a fault is detected, the system may generate an alert, which is an indication that a fault has occurred. An alarm signifies an undesirable state in a resource that requires corrective action. An alarm is often triggered by the transition to an alarmed state and may result in a continuous visual or auditory indication (such as a red light or beeping) to draw an operator's attention.

The relationship is: a fault leads to an alert; the transition to an alarmed state may result in an alert being issued; the receipt of that alert may trigger an alarm condition in the operator's console. An incident is an undesired occurrence resulting from one or more problems—for example, unexpected interruption of a network service or degradation of service quality.
sections.eli5: When something breaks, the system sends an alert. If it is serious, an alarm goes off to get someone's attention.

sections.title: A Fault Management Workflow
sections.content:
Consider an example: a link goes down (a fault). The network monitoring system detects this event, evaluates it as relevant, and labels it an occurrence. Because it is undesired, it is a fault. The system generates an alert. If the link is critical and service is interrupted, an alarm is triggered in the operator's console. The operator investigates and finds that the link suffered a fiber microbend (the cause). The underlying problem is not just "link is down" but "this link has a physical problem." The operator repairs the fiber and the link comes back up (resolving the service incident), but the broader problem—"something caused a microbend"—must be investigated further to prevent recurrence. Once the root cause is understood and measures are put in place to prevent it, the problem is resolved.

This example shows that problems may have multiple layers: the immediate impact (service interruption), the direct cause (physical fiber damage), and deeper root causes (environmental or installation issues). Effective fault management addresses all layers.
sections.eli5: A link breaks (fault), the operator notices (alert), service is affected (alarm), the operator finds the cause and fixes it, then investigates why it happened in the first place.
